soil-chem-202.title: Ionic strength: why a doubly charged ion counts fourfold
soil-chem-202.text: Dissolve magnesium sulfate in water and it counts for four times as much as the same concentration of table salt. The yardstick is ionic strength, a measure of the ions in a solution weighted by their charge. In molar form it is I = ½ Σ ci zi², summed over every ion, where c is molar concentration and z the ion's charge number. Squaring the charge makes multivalent ions weigh heavily: for NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration, while MgSO4 gives four times as much. It can be molar or molal, so units should be stated, and molality is preferred for non-ideal solutions. In {{ref:soil-found-079}}, total electrolyte concentration shifts dissociation constants and the solubility of salts. It also sets the Debye length, the thickness scale of the charged double layer around a surface. That length is inversely proportional to the square root of ionic strength, so more or higher-valence counterions compress the layer. Lewis and Randall introduced the concept in 1921, while describing how strong electrolytes depart from ideal behavior.

soil-chem-201.title: Activity coefficients: correcting for crowded ions
soil-chem-201.text: Soil water is crowded. Small volumes of it hold high concentrations of electrolytes, which is why activity coefficients matter so much in soil chemistry. An activity coefficient is a factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behavior. Activity equals the coefficient times concentration. In an ideal electrolyte solution every coefficient equals one, a state only very dilute solutions approach. As concentration rises, ions interact more and the coefficients change. Cation and anion values cannot be measured separately, so chemists use a mean activity coefficient, γ±. Even pH rests on this limit: it is defined from hydrogen ion activity, a definition IUPAC calls only notional. Coefficients come from the Debye–Hückel equation or its extensions, the Davies and Pitzer equations, or from specific ion interaction theory. Uncharged species such as dissolved CO2 follow a salting-out model, log10 γ = bI, with b for CO2 0.11 at 10 °C.

soil-chem-203.title: Debye and Hückel explain why salt water misbehaves
soil-chem-203.text: Unlike charges attract and like charges repel, and in a salt solution that simple rule spoils the arithmetic. Ions are not scattered at random, so the solution departs from ideal behavior. Debye–Hückel theory, published by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel in 1923 in Physikalische Zeitschrift, explains why. It pictures each ion surrounded by a statistically averaged cloud of net opposite charge. It assumes complete dissociation, spherical unpolarized ions and a solvent that acts only as a medium of constant permittivity. The result, a linearized Poisson–Boltzmann model, predicts mean ionic activity coefficients accurately in dilute solution. Its limiting law makes the logarithm of the mean activity coefficient proportional to the square root of {{ref:soil-chem-202}}. That law fits measurements below about 10⁻³ mol/L but drifts at higher concentrations and with more highly charged ions. The extended equation holds up to ionic strength 0.1; beyond that, the Pitzer equations should be used. The theory still underlies modern treatments.

soil-chem-208.title: Inner sphere complexes: ions that bond straight to minerals
soil-chem-208.text: Some ions hover near a mineral surface; others grab it. In an inner sphere complex, an ion binds directly to the surface with no water molecules between them. In an outer sphere complex, water keeps the two apart. Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form the inner kind, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently. Surface hydroxyl groups act as electron-donating ligands. On oxide surfaces the metal ion is a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor, and the ligand a Lewis base, an electron-pair donor. Sorption of protonated ligands therefore depends on pH. These complexes govern how trace elements move or stay put in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides. Sulfate held this way can slow or prevent the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides. Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ions get larger, so they grow more mobile during weathering. Through such bonds, soil properties decide whether nutrients and pollutants are retained or lost.

soil-chem-206.title: Langmuir's model: one molecule per parking space
soil-chem-206.text: Irving Langmuir won the 1932 Nobel Prize for his surface chemistry, and one idea from it still opens most adsorption studies. The Langmuir adsorption model pictures a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one molecule, with adsorption and its reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, both possible. Each binding is a reaction between a molecule and an empty site, with an equilibrium constant K. The fraction of occupied sites is θ = K p / (1 + K p). At low pressure θ is about Kp; at high pressure θ approaches 1 as the single layer fills. The model assumes a flat, uniform surface, immobile molecules, equal energy at every site and no interaction between neighbors. Real surfaces are rough, with several site types, and adsorbed molecules do interact, so it often deviates. A competitive form lets two species vie for the same sites. Langmuir presented it in 1916, and it remains the first choice for most adsorption models.

soil-chem-209.title: Partition coefficients: how a compound splits between liquids
soil-chem-209.text: Shake a compound with water and octanol, and it divides itself between the two layers. The partition coefficient is the ratio of its concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium. With water and octanol, it measures how water-loving or water-shunning a substance is. Hydrogeologists use this octanol–water coefficient, Kow, to predict how dissolved hydrophobic organic compounds migrate in soil and groundwater. Strictly it covers only the un-ionized form, while the distribution coefficient covers all forms. One or both phases can even be solid.

soil-chem-204.title: Coprecipitation: solids that drag dissolved metals down
soil-chem-204.text: A forming precipitate can carry down substances that would otherwise stay dissolved. That is coprecipitation. The captured material may sit inside the crystal lattice, be sealed in as the crystal grows, or cling to the precipitate's surface. Trace elements too dilute to precipitate alone ride down with a carrier of similar crystal structure. The process matters in {{ref:soil-bio-059}}, in heavy metal transport, wastewater treatment and radionuclide migration around waste repositories. Wetlands built for treatment, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-260}}, remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminum and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants strip arsenic from water the same way.

soil-chem-205.title: The Freundlich equation, a rule fitted to rough surfaces
soil-chem-205.text: Freundlich fitted his equation to organic acids adsorbing on coal from water, and it outlived that modest start. The Freundlich equation, dating from 1909, is an empirical adsorption isotherm. It links the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration. It reads x/m = K c^(1/n), where x/m is adsorbate mass per adsorbent mass and K and n are constants for a given pair at a given temperature. In log form, log x/m = log K + (1/n) log c, it becomes a straight line. It can also be derived from an uneven surface: high-energy sites fill first, then weaker ones, so the heat of adsorption falls as coverage grows. A good fit makes such a surface likely, not proved; calorimetry can confirm it. The equation fails at high pressure, where adsorption saturates. Being empirical, it should give way to theory-based isotherms such as Langmuir's or BET when those fit.

soil-chem-210.title: X-ray absorption fine structure reveals an atom's neighbors
soil-chem-210.text: An X-ray absorption spectrum carries fine detail that maps the surroundings of a single kind of atom. This X-ray absorption fine structure divides into the edge, the XANES region spanning 50–100 eV around the threshold, and the EXAFS region; XAFS means the two together. EXAFS arises as the ejected photoelectron scatters once off neighboring atoms, giving local structure. Multiple-scattering peaks in XANES give its geometry. Surface EXAFS reveals the coordination and chemical state of adsorbed ions. With X-ray diffraction, both methods show how microbes sorb and mineralize radionuclides when they are used to clean up contamination, as in {{ref:soil-env-023}}.

soil-chem-211.title: Chemical speciation: naming every form an element takes
soil-chem-211.text: Knowing how much of a metal a solution holds says little about what form it takes. Chemical speciation is the calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present. Geochemical equilibrium models predict them from measurements of bulk solution composition, for plant nutrients in soil and for regulated metals in stored wastes. Trace metals form complexes with hydroxide, carbonate and chloride, and their speciation changes between oxidized and reduced conditions. An element's toxicity also depends on how oxidized it is, so food regulations require speciation of some elements.

soil-chem-207.title: Geochemical models, from hand sums to reactive transport
soil-chem-207.text: In 1962 Garrels and Thompson built a geochemical model by hand. From a solution's bulk composition, they predicted its species, its saturation with each mineral and the fugacities of its gases. Geochemical modeling now does this mostly by computer, using thermodynamics, kinetics or both to analyze reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature waters near Earth's surface. A model starts from a basis of aqueous species, minerals and gases, as many as the system has components. It then solves mass action and mass balance equations for equilibrium. A mineral's saturation index, log Q/K, is zero at equilibrium, positive when the mineral is likely to precipitate and negative when it tends to dissolve. Helgeson's 1968 program added mass transfer, creating reaction path models of processes such as weathering. Linking to water-flow models gives reactive transport along a flowpath. Uses run from {{ref:soil-chem-211}} of plant nutrients to contaminant mobility in groundwater. One weakness is seldom considered: thermodynamic databases differ, causing large uncertainties.

openers.soil-solution-chemistry-and-sorption: Soil water is never pure. It carries crowds of ions that shield and jostle one another, and it bathes mineral surfaces that grab some of those ions and let others pass. This chapter follows that traffic: how chemists weigh a solution's charged load, correct for ions that do not behave ideally, and describe how substances bind to surfaces or get swept into a forming solid. It ends with the tools that tie the picture together: X-ray spectra that show an atom's immediate surroundings, and computer models that calculate every species in a solution and the reactions among them.

reviews.soil-solution-chemistry-and-sorption: Ionic strength weighs a solution's ions by their charge, and the activity coefficient corrects for how those ions crowd one another. Debye–Hückel theory explains the gap with clouds of opposite charge and links the two through a square-root law. At mineral surfaces, ions in inner sphere complexes bind directly, while Langmuir's model fills identical sites one molecule each and the Freundlich equation fits uneven surfaces whose strong sites fill first. Partition coefficients and coprecipitation trace other routes out of solution, into a second liquid or a growing solid. X-ray absorption fine structure shows how adsorbed atoms sit, and speciation calculations and geochemical models join it all, solving for every species and mineral at once.
